questions.question: What is a political party, and how do parties try to win elections?
questions.expected_answer: A political party is an organised group of people who share similar ideas about how the country should be run and who want to win elections to form the government. Parties write manifestos explaining what they will do if they win, and campaign by holding rallies, putting up posters, speaking on radio and television and visiting voters door to door. Opposition parties watch the government and criticise its mistakes.

questions.question: Describe how people voted in the 1994 election.
questions.expected_answer: The election was run by the Independent Electoral Commission. Special votes were held on the twenty-sixth of April for the elderly, sick, disabled and South Africans abroad, and the main voting day was the twenty-seventh, with voting extended in some areas. Voters had to be citizens aged eighteen or older with ID or a temporary voter's card. Their hands were checked under a special light and marked with invisible ink. They received two ballot papers, with party names, symbols and leaders' photos, and made a secret cross behind a screen.

questions.question: Explain proportional representation and describe the results of the 1994 election.
questions.expected_answer: In proportional representation, people vote for a party, and each party gets a share of the four hundred National Assembly seats that matches its share of the votes, filling them from a list. In 1994, the ANC won about sixty-two per cent, the National Party about twenty per cent and the IFP about ten per cent, with smaller parties such as the Freedom Front, Democratic Party, PAC and ACDP also winning seats. The ANC formed the government with Mandela as President.
